title: The Bias of a Gyro When the Robot Stops: Knowing That It Is Still, Reading the Bias From a Few Seconds of Stillness, and How Often a Robot Must Stop to Keep Its Heading

questions.question: What should a gyro read when the robot is standing still?
options: Its last reading before it stopped
The earth's rotation only, which is its bias
Zero, exactly, if it is a good one
Nothing: so what it does read is the bias plus noise
questions.explanation: A robot that is not turning has no turn rate to report. Whatever the gyro says then is its own bias, with noise on top.

questions.question: A detector that looked at the wheels alone said still for how many of 200 samples of a robot being carried?
questions.explanation: Its wheels were stopped while it swung in someone's hands. Asking the accelerometer to be quiet as well brought it to 0.

questions.question: The bias read from a stop of 10 s was good to:
options: 0.005 rad/s, the noise of one reading
questions.explanation: The gyro's noise of 0.005 rad/s over the root of the number of samples. One second gave 0.00063 and ten seconds 0.00020.

questions.question: With a stop of 2 s every 10 s the heading ended out by:
questions.explanation: The bias walks, so a reading goes stale. Read once it left 9.9 degrees after 300 s; every 60 s, 4.6; every 10 s, 0.8.

questions.question: Why does the detector wait for a whole window?
options: The gyro needs time to warm up
The filter needs 25 samples to start
questions.explanation: A robot can pass through zero speed without being at rest. Half a second of quiet wheels and a quiet accelerometer is the evidence.

questions.question: What found the step in the bias?
options: The next stop, which read the gyro again
questions.explanation: The bias stepped by 0.01 rad/s at 100 s and was read again 19 s later, when the robot next stood still.
